title: KV cache + batching sprint scratchpad
body:
Quick context and intent:
- Sprint goal (2 weeks): get an experimental baseline for lightweight KV compression + more aggressive continuous batching heuristics on 8xA100 Dedicated dev cluster. Want to quantify latency regressions vs token-cost wins and cache hit tradeoffs.
- This doc: messy running notes, micro-summaries of relevant papers/blog posts, experiments to run, and open questions.

Papers / posts I pulled together (very rough reads):
1) FlashAttention v2 / memory-eff improvements (2023-2025 followups) — short: shows that attention kernel fusion + tiled IO can cut memory pressure and speed up backward/forward, but not directly addressing KV cache storage on host. Takeaway: leverage fused kernels where possible, but swapping patterns for large KV caches still bottlenecked by host<->device bandwidth.
2) "Compressing KV Caches for Long Contexts" (preprint, Nov 2025) — proposes top-k sparse sketch + product quantization for old KV entries; stores compressed representation with occasional full-resolution rehydration. Reported 2.2x reduction in KV memory with <1% perplexity loss on eval prompts.
3) MoE routing papers (routing-cost tradeoffs) — useful ideas for routing requests to shards/variants to minimize cross-node KV reads. Not directly KV compression but the routing heuristics seem adaptable to choose between full-KV vs compressed-KV replicas.
4) DeepSpeed-Serving writeups and blog experiments re: batching thresholds and end-to-end latency SLOs — pragmatic heuristics for continuous batching (e.g., max-wait ms, adaptive slack based on recent latency tail).

Notes / quick summaries (my brain dump):
- KV compression idea matrix:
  - Full PQ (product quant) on keys only, keep values in fp16: cheaper storage, but rehydration cost (dequant + matmul) may spike latency.
  - Sparse delta encoding (store dense for recent window, deltas for older entries): good if recency dominates cache hits.
  - LRU + checkpointing: evict and checkpoint to host when not needed; bring back on demand. Good for very long contexts but increases tail latency.
  - Bloom-filter indexed segments: to quickly decide whether compressed segment likely contains hits (to avoid decomp).

- Continuous batching heuristics to test:
  - Fixed max-wait (ms) vs adaptive: adaptive increases max-wait when system is underutilized, reduces under load.
  - Per-customer priority buckets: high-SLA routes bypass batching or have smaller wait windows.
  - Early-start streaming + partial generation: start token generation as soon as prefix ready while waiting for remaining batch members' full KV preprocessing. Risk: inconsistent outputs if KV states differ.

Experiment plan (minimal, prioritized):
1) Baseline: no compression, existing batching policy (max-wait 6ms). Measure: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU mem usage, host mem usage, observed KV hit distribution across context positions.
2) PQ-on-keys prototype: compress keys to 8-bit PQ (4 subquantizers) locally. Keep values fp16. Measure additional CPU/GPU overhead for decompress and impact on p95/p99. Run across inference lengths 512, 2048, 8192.
3) Delta window (recent dense 1024, compressed beyond): measure hit ratio across positions and tail latencies.
4) Adaptive batching toggle: implement simple PID-ish controller that adjusts max-wait based on p95 vs target. Compare cost/TPS and percentage of requests served within SLO.
5) Combined: PQ + adaptive batching. Measure cost per million tokens and latency tail.

Things I saw in early runs (prelim):
- PQ prototype dropped GPU mem by ~28% for 8k contexts on a small 2-model sample, but p99 increased ~35ms on average because of decompression kernel launching on CPU->GPU syncs. Need a fully GPU-side dequant path.
- Adaptive batching reduced overall cost by ~6% in low-concurrency sims, but under bursty load it occasionally added to p99 because controller tuned poorly.

Open engineering questions / risks:
- Can we implement PQ dequant entirely on device (CUDA kernels) and avoid host sync? Likely yes but needs kernel engineering and careful memory layout.
- How to measure consistency/regression vs quality? Need a small prompt-set suite (200 prompts) to measure exact match / logprob deltas; tie to Redwood Optimize eval pipeline.
- When compressed KV misses and we rehydrate, do we cause head-of-line blocking? Need to simulate rehydration costs and perhaps allow speculative fallbacks to smaller models if rehydration would violate SLO.
- Does compression interact badly with streaming clients? If we compress prefix KV but client subscribes to streaming tokens, rehydration latency could delay first token. Maybe allow streaming if recent dense window covers needed context.

Actionable TODOs (for me / Owen / Lena):
- [Sophia] Instrument current serving runtime to export per-request KV age histogram and per-model cache hit stats (ticket: RINF-5123).
- [Owen] Prototype simple GPU PQ dequant kernel or find baseline kernel from existing repo (check deepobs repo) — estimate effort 3-5d.
- [Lena] Build small eval suite of 200 prompts spanning conversational, code, and long-context summarization; wire into Redwood Optimize quick-eval so we can get automated quality metrics.
- Run combined PQ + adaptive batching smoke test on dev Dedicated (8xA100) — aim for first run by 2026-03-05.

Unresolved product questions to raise with PMs:
- Are we willing to accept a small p99 latency bump for 30–50% KV memory reduction on Dedicated customers? Which customer tiers get compression-by-default vs opt-in?
- For Private deployments, what operational constraints exist around deploying experimental kernels (e.g., external binary restrictions)?

Random notes / heuristics I liked:
- "Compress old, keep recent dense" seems low-risk: most hits are near prefix, so we pay for accuracy where it matters.
- Expose compression policy per-model route in Console with obvious knobs (recent-window, quant-bits, fallback-policy). Helps platform teams tune per-app.

Links I bookmarked (quick):
- FlashAttention (original): https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135
- PQ survey blog (practical quantization tips): https://distill.pub/2025/quantization-primer (bookmark, may be internal-only)
- Internal PR for early PQ experiment: https://github.com/redwood-inference/kv-compression-experiments/pull/23

Closing thoughts:
- This is messy but promising. Biggest engineering lift is moving any decompression work onto GPUs and making it non-blocking. If we can do that, combined with adaptive batching we could meaningfully reduce Dedicated unit-costs for long-context workloads without heavy quality regressions.
- Will keep iterating; next update after baseline instrumentation and first PQ GPU prototype run.

-- Sophia
